opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it helps to step back and ask what mathematics is actually *for*. There's a temptation to picture it as a big pile of true statements, where the job of a mathematician is to add more of them. But there are infinitely many true statements, and almost all of them are utterly boring. You could have a machine churning out a proven theorem every microsecond, things like "this particular enormous number is not prime," and you'd have made essentially no mathematical progress at all. The space of truths is vast, and the valuable part is a vanishingly thin slice of it.

So the scarce resource was never really the ability to grind through a proof. It's the judgment about which questions are worth asking: which ones connect different areas, which ones reveal some deeper structure, which ones would unlock a whole family of other results, or which ones matter for physics or computer science or how we understand the world. When Riemann posed his hypothesis, or when people started asking about the structure of the primes in the first place, the act of framing was where much of the insight lay.

There's also the question of understanding. A proof that's a billion steps long, verified by a machine, might settle whether something is true, but it may not tell any human *why* it's true. And a lot of what mathematicians value is that sense of illumination, of seeing why things have to be the way they are. So even in a world of extremely fast automated proving, someone or something has to be steering. It has to decide what to aim at, and turn the results into understanding we can actually use.

Now, I don't want to be complacent here. It's quite possible that AI systems will also get good at choosing interesting questions. Taste isn't magic, and there's no law saying only humans can have it. But I think it's a mistake to treat raw proving speed as if it were the whole of mathematics. It's a bit like thinking that a printing press that could print a million pages a second would make writing obsolete. The bottleneck was always deciding what's worth saying.

r001.rationale: The response says there are infinitely many true statements and that proving one per microsecond would add little progress, but it does not clearly state that their sheer number makes exhaustive enumeration impractical at that rate.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes rapid proving from deciding which questions are worth pursuing, and says proving speed alone does not settle the need for question selection.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the thing people often miss is that the set of true mathematical statements is effectively infinite, and almost all of them are completely worthless. You could have a machine generating theorems at an astonishing rate, and if it's just working through the space of provable statements, the overwhelming majority of what it produces would be things like "this particular sum equals this particular number" — true, verifiable, and of no interest to anyone. So the bottleneck isn't really proof, it's selection.

And when you look at what mathematicians actually value, a lot of it is about the question rather than the answer. The reason Fermat's Last Theorem mattered wasn't that anyone urgently needed to know whether those equations had solutions. It was that the question sat at this junction where answering it required building entire new areas of mathematics, connecting things that didn't seem connected. A good question is one that, when you pull on it, something else moves. Knowing which threads to pull is a different skill from being able to pull them.

There's also a point about what mathematics is for, in a sense. Part of it is instrumental — we want results we can use in physics or cryptography or wherever. But a large part of it is about understanding, about humans coming to see why something is true, not just that it's true. If I hand you a hundred-thousand-page machine-generated proof, you've got a certificate that the statement holds, but you may not have gained any understanding at all. So even with unlimited proving power, there's this further question of which results would actually illuminate things for us, which proofs would be the kind we could learn from. And choosing for that is a matter of taste and judgment about what's deep.

Now, I should say — I don't think this is necessarily something only humans can do. It's quite possible AI systems get good at mathematical taste too. But I think it's a genuinely separate capability, and it's one we have much less of a handle on. We know what it means for a proof to be correct. We have a much weaker grip on what it means for a question to be interesting, and so I'd expect that to remain the hard and valuable part for a good while, even in a world where verification is essentially free.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematical statements are effectively infinite and mostly worthless, but does not state that exhaustive enumeration would be impractical even at one proof per microsecond.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes rapid proving from selecting interesting questions, describing mathematical taste as a separate capability and saying AI may or may not develop it.

astra-6.text:
Well, because there are vastly more mathematical statements than there are interesting mathematical statements. You could generate endless true statements by doing arithmetic with larger and larger numbers, but that wouldn’t necessarily advance our understanding. The question is which things are worth proving — which reveal some deeper structure, or connect areas that previously seemed unrelated.

So even if proving things became extraordinarily cheap, there would still be this question of where to direct that ability. In fact, choosing the questions might become a larger part of the intellectual work. That doesn’t mean an AI couldn’t also become good at choosing them. But the ability to prove a statement very quickly doesn’t, by itself, tell you which statements matter.

r001.rationale: It notes there are vastly more statements than interesting ones, but does not say exhaustive enumeration would be impractical at one proof per microsecond.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, proving statements isn’t quite the same thing as advancing mathematics. There are infinitely many statements you could prove that are utterly uninteresting — consequences of things we already know, or facts that don’t help us understand anything else. So even if you could produce a proof every microsecond, you’d still need to decide where to direct that ability.

What makes a question interesting might be that it connects two areas that seemed unrelated, or that answering it would give us a powerful new way of thinking. And there’s a question of which results are worth a human’s time to understand. If proofs become extraordinarily cheap, our attention could become the bottleneck.

An AI might also become very good at choosing those questions. But that wouldn’t make the choice unimportant. It would mean that the AI was doing another important part of mathematics, beyond proving the statements it was given.

r001.rationale: The response says there are infinitely many uninteresting statements and that someone must choose where to direct proof effort. It does not state that exhaustive enumeration is impractical because of the volume, even at one proof per microsecond.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes proving statements from choosing which questions matter, and says an AI’s skill at proving would not make question selection unimportant.
